sections.section_title: Freedom, and What Circumcision Would Cost
sections.summary: Paul commands the Galatians to hold the position Christ won for them and states in the letter's most emphatic language that accepting circumcision would enroll them as debtors to the whole law, sever them from Christ, and drop them out of grace.
sections.relevance: The neutral reading takes 5:4 as the plainest statement in the letter of what the conversion programme would cost, and it is Paul's own argument rather than an illustration: katergeo (aorist passive) breaks a connection to a person, not a benefit, and ekpipto describes falling out of the sphere of grace where the Galatians were standing. The reading is careful about the grammar: neither verb describes a possession confiscated or a credit reversed, which is a different shape from what a reader's prior theology tends to supply in either direction. It also notes two counterweights within the same section -- the present tense of 'you who would be justified by law' describes people in the act rather than people who have arrived, and 5:5 places righteousness among things eagerly awaited rather than only already held, a tension the reading declines to resolve. 5:6's 'faith working through love' further rules out treating standing as an inert state.
key_phrases: stand firm therefore
do not submit again to a yoke of slavery
Christ will be of no benefit to you
he is a debtor to do the whole law
you are severed from Christ
you have fallen from grace
we eagerly await the hope of righteousness
faith working through love

sections.summary: Paul asks who cut across the Galatians' course, denies that the campaign of persuasion comes from the God who calls them, cites the leaven proverb, states his confidence that they will take no other view, and ends with a bitter wish about the other teachers.
sections.relevance: The section is chiefly an attack on the other teachers, but its images bear on the question sideways. The imperfect 'you were running well' describes a course that was going well and was then obstructed, and the leaven proverb denies that a single accepted requirement can be contained -- both presuppose that a believing community's position can be spoiled from where it stood. Against that, 5:10 is what the neutral reading calls the most hopeful sentence in the letter, and it locates the ground of Paul's confidence outside the congregations ('in the Lord') while the present participle 'him who calls you' has God still calling. The reading insists both registers belong to the same paragraph, so the section does not settle the question on its own.
key_phrases: you were running well
who cut in on you
a little leaven leavens the whole lump
I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view
him who calls you

sections.summary: The letter turns at 5:13 from what the Galatians must not do to what they should: freedom is what they were called into, and it is not to become a base of operations for the flesh but is discharged as mutual slavery in love, the whole law standing fulfilled in Leviticus 19:18.
sections.relevance: The reading treats 5:13 as the hinge of the letter and states its logic directly: freedom here is not the absence of obligation but the transfer of it -- a servitude freely given replacing one exacted as the price of standing. That bears on the question because it forecloses reading the letter's freedom as release from accountability, and because aphorme (a fortified base from which a campaign is launched) warns that freedom can be actively used for the flesh rather than merely misunderstood. The closing warning that they may be consumed by one another is a consequence-warning within the believing community, though the consumption in view is communal destruction rather than a stated loss of standing.
key_phrases: you were called to freedom
do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh
through love serve one another
the whole law is fulfilled in one word
watch out that you are not consumed by one another

sections.summary: Paul commands walking by the Spirit with a categorical promise attached, describes flesh and Spirit as standing opposed like armies drawn up against each other, and says that those led by the Spirit are not under law.
sections.relevance: Everything favourable here is stated conditionally: the ou me promise ('you will certainly not carry out the desire of the flesh') is attached to a command, and 'you are not under law' hangs on the present passive 'if you are being led by the Spirit,' an ongoing condition rather than a settled acquisition. The reading stresses that peripateo is the Jewish idiom for daily conduct step by step, 'not of a stance or a state,' and that the verse's placement immediately before a list of behaviours that forfeit the kingdom is what keeps it from being read as release from obligation. The section itself does not say standing can be lost; its conditional grammar is what leans.
key_phrases: walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh
these are opposed to each other
if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under law

sections.summary: Paul names fifteen works of the flesh -- eight of them concerning the breakdown of relations within a group -- and repeats a warning he had already given them, that those who practise such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
sections.relevance: This is Paul's own argument, not an aside, and the neutral reading is explicit that the addressees are the same people addressed throughout the letter: those who received the Spirit (3:2), who are sons of God (3:26), who are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise (3:29), in whose hearts the Spirit cries Abba. The warning is therefore about believers and about the inheritance they were said to hold. Two details shape it rather than soften it: the present participle 'those who practise' denotes a settled way of going on rather than a single act, and the warning is expressed as an inheritance not entered -- the same grammar the reading traces through 5:4 and 6:8-9, in which nothing is confiscated but a relation is departed from or a destination not reached. The list is aimed at a congregation already biting and devouring one another (5:15), so the warning is live rather than hypothetical.
key_phrases: the works of the flesh are evident
I warn you, as I warned you before
those who practise such things
will not inherit the kingdom of God

sections.summary: Paul sets the singular fruit of the Spirit against the plural works of the flesh, says there is no law against such things, states that those who belong to Christ crucified the flesh with its passions and desires, and calls the community to keep in step with the Spirit rather than provoke and envy one another.
sections.relevance: This section supplies the chapter's main counterweight to its warnings. 5:24 is an aorist describing a completed act, and the reading notes that crucifixion is the letter's recurring image for a decisive and irreversible severance, involving participation in Christ's death rather than a separate act alongside it. 5:25's structure is the section's whole logic on the reading's account -- the indicative comes first and the imperative follows from it, so they are told to become what they already are, which is a standing presupposed rather than earned by the conduct enjoined. What keeps this from being stronger is that the section is cast almost entirely as exhortation, that the believers themselves are the subject of the crucifying, and that the imperatives assume keeping in step is not automatic. Categorized as leaning permanent on the priority of the indicative, with the ambiguity real.
key_phrases: the fruit of the Spirit
against such things there is no law
those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh
if we live by the Spirit, let us also walk in line by the Spirit
provoking one another, envying one another
